strengths: The paper offers a well-structured theoretical contribution: Theorem 3.2 gives a sufficient-and-necessary characterization of the optimal per-step low-rank adapters (via truncated SVD of the gradient), and the restriction to scalar/column-wise scaling yields closed-form global optima (Theorems 3.5 and 3.7) at only O((m+n+r)r^2) overhead. The proofs (Appendix A) are complete and appear correct, building on Eckart-Young and standard smoothness assumptions.

The observation that column-wise scaling preserves equivariance of Adam(W) moment estimators (Lemmas 3.3 and 3.6) is a practically important insight: it enables high-rank accumulation without optimizer restarts or learning-rate re-warmup, directly addressing the key drawback of ReLoRA.

Experimental coverage is broad and includes strong recent baselines (ReLoRA, LoRA-GA, MoRA, HiRA) across four models (DeBERTaV3-base up to Gemma-3-12B) and three task families (GLUE, commonsense reasoning, math), with overhead measurements (Figure 3, Table 5) and multiple ablations (intermittent interval I, scalar vs. column scaling, rank/rank-growth analysis in Tables 3 and 10-11).

The paper is honest about limitations: the ~50% per-step time overhead of full ScaLoRA, the partial applicability of the column-wise optimality condition (~80% of layers), and the storage of the merged weight matrix are all explicitly discussed, and the ScaLoRA-I variant is a sensible mitigation backed by an ablation.

Diagnostics such as gradient rank (Figure 2c), rank growth of the cumulative update (Figure 2b), and layer-wise patterns of scaling choice (Figure 5) empirically validate the assumptions behind the theorems and provide mechanistic insight into why the method works.
weaknesses: The notion of 'optimal' adapters is derived only for a one-step quadratic upper bound (6)-(7) under plain GD dynamics, while the actual algorithm uses AdamW and the O(eta^2) terms are discarded. There is no convergence analysis of the full ScaLoRA algorithm; claims of 'provably' fast convergence rest entirely on empirical curves. The optimality is w.r.t. a bound whose key constant (1/L) is admittedly treated as a tuned hyperparameter, weakening the theoretical punchline.

Performance gains over strong baselines are modest and sometimes within reported standard deviations. On GLUE the average margin over HiRA is ~0.5%, and on LLaMA3-8B commonsense reasoning ScaLoRA's 77.85 vs. HiRA's 77.46 and MoRA's 77.27 are small; several cells in Table 2 show overlapping error bars. The claimed 'superior performance' would benefit from significance testing.

The column-wise optimality in Theorem 3.7 holds only when a non-negativity condition on the 2r x 2r linear system is met; when it fails the method silently falls back to scalar scaling, so the headline theoretical guarantee covers only a fraction of iterations in practice.

MoRA and HiRA are excluded from the math problem-solving experiments (Table 4) 'due to their limited scalability', yet both were runnable on LLaMA3-8B where they were competitive; this asymmetric exclusion weakens the comparison on the largest model.

Several experimental details raise fairness/reproducibility questions: HiRA and LoRA-GA learning rates are rescaled by ad-hoc factors (10x and 1/10x), epoch counts are reduced for ScaLoRA ('The number epochs are reduced due to the fast convergence'), and the rank metric uses an undocumented 0.005 singular-value threshold. No code release or link is stated in the manuscript, limiting reproducibility despite the detailed hyperparameter tables.

The extra O(mnr) merge operation and dependence on eta and the Lipschitz constant L in the optimal scaling factors add hyperparameter sensitivity, and the per-step optimality may not compose into per-run optimality; this gap between one-step and trajectory-level guarantees is not discussed in depth.

strengths: The paper provides a principled framing of high-rank updates: characterizing the per-step optimal low-rank adapters via a quadratic upper bound on the loss (Theorem 3.2), with a clean necessary-and-sufficient condition connecting the optimum to a truncated rank-2r SVD of the gradient.

The analytical results for scalar scaling (Theorem 3.5) and column-wise scaling (Theorem 3.7) are worked out carefully, with full proofs in the appendix, and the moment-estimator transfer lemmas (3.3, 3.6) address a genuine practical obstacle (optimizer state continuity when swapping adapters).

The empirical evaluation is broad: GLUE (DeBERTaV3-base), commonsense reasoning (LLaMA2-7B, LLaMA3-8B), and math (Gemma-3-12B), with SOTA high-rank baselines (ReLoRA, LoRA-GA, MoRA, HiRA) and useful diagnostics (rank/stable-rank of updates, memory/time overhead, non-negativity frequency, per-layer scaling patterns).

Complexity analysis (Table 5) and the amortized ScaLoRA-I variant with an ablation on I are appropriate and honest about the method's time cost; limitations (time, storage of the merged matrix) are explicitly discussed.
weaknesses: There is a significant gap between theory and practice. All optimality guarantees are derived for plain GD under a quadratic upper bound with a Lipschitz constant L that is admittedly uncomputable and treated as a tuned hyperparameter, yet the actual algorithm uses Adam(W). The 'optimal' scalings are therefore only optimal for a surrogate objective whose assumptions (negligible O(η^2) terms, fixed L) may not hold, so the central claim of 'optimally scaled' adapters is only weakly supported in the regime that matters.

The column-wise optimality result (Theorem 3.7) holds only when the 2r×2r linear system has a non-negative solution, which the authors report holds for only ~80% of layers/iterations; the fallback to scalar scaling is unprincipled relative to the claimed guarantees, and the overall mixed scheme lacks any convergence guarantee of its own.

Empirical gains are modest and sometimes within noise. On GLUE the average improvement over HiRA is ~0.5% with overlapping standard deviations on several tasks; on commonsense reasoning the margin over HiRA/ReLoRA is ~0.4–0.6%, and ScaLoRA-I is often statistically indistinguishable from LoRA-GA on individual tasks. Given the ~50%+ runtime increase of ScaLoRA (only mitigated by the I=10 variant that loses part of the gain), the cost-benefit case is not compelling.

The storage limitation is more serious than presented: ScaLoRA must materialize and store the merged W_t = W_pt + A_t B_t^T for every adapted matrix, which conflicts with the core PEFT premise of avoiding full-size trainable/updated weight tensors and undermines comparability of the reported memory numbers with LoRA-style methods.

The contribution is incremental relative to ReLoRA: the main novelty is a principled choice of the re-parameterized adapters between merges, but the merge-and-refactor skeleton, the restart problem, and the high-rank-accumulation motivation are inherited from prior work (ReLoRA, LoRA-GA as a special case acknowledged by the authors).

Theoretical assumptions are under-validated beyond a single small dataset: rank(∇ℓ) ≥ 2r and the non-negativity condition are only checked on RTE (Figure 2), a tiny task, and it is unclear whether they hold for large models on hard tasks where the method is claimed to matter most.

Some experimental comparisons are not fully controlled: MoRA and HiRA are excluded from convergence/rank plots due to different learning rates, HiRA learning rates are rescaled by 10×, and epoch counts are reduced for ScaLoRA ('number of epochs are reduced due to the fast convergence of ScaLoRA'), which complicates attribution of the gains.

No code release or artifact is mentioned, which limits reproducibility of a method whose implementation involves several nontrivial details (moment transfer, in-place merging, mixed scalar/column switching).

strengths: The core idea is well motivated and clearly articulated: instead of LoRA's fixed low-rank subspace, ScaLoRA merges the current adapter into the frozen weights and re-factors a scaled low-rank adapter each step, avoiding ReLoRA-style restarts and optimizer resets.

The theoretical contribution is non-trivial and fairly complete: Theorem 3.2 gives a sufficient and necessary condition for the optimal adapters (revealing that the ideal choice requires a rank-2r truncated SVD of the gradient), and Theorems 3.5 and 3.7 derive closed-form global optimizers for scalar and column-wise scaling. Proofs are provided and largely self-contained, correctly exploiting Eckart-Young and Schur product tools.

The treatment of adaptive optimizers is a thoughtful, practical detail: Lemmas 3.3 and 3.6 show that gradient moment estimators transform equivariantly under (column-wise) scaling, which is exactly what makes the merge-and-rescale scheme compatible with AdamW without warm-up restarts.

Experiments are reasonably broad: GLUE with DeBERTaV3-base, eight commonsense reasoning tasks with LLaMA2-7B and LLaMA3-8B, and math tasks with Gemma-3-12B, against relevant baselines (LoRA, ReLoRA, LoRA-GA, MoRA, HiRA). The ablations (choice of I, scalar vs. column scaling, layer-level scaling patterns) and the rank/stable-rank analysis (Table 3) meaningfully support the claimed mechanism.
Efficiency and storage limitations are discussed honestly (time overhead of merging, need for ScaLoRA-I, storage of merged matrices), which increases trust in the reported trade-offs.
Empirical validation of the theory (Figures 2c/2d for the rank and non-negativity assumptions) connects analysis to practice.
weaknesses: There is a gap between what is proven and what the algorithm does. The 'optimality' results characterize minimizers of a quadratic upper bound of the loss under plain GD, whereas the method is run with AdamW on adapters. The per-step choice is only greedy-optimal with respect to a surrogate; no convergence guarantee is given for the actual ScaLoRA/ScaLoRA-I procedure (e.g., cumulative loss descent or a rank-growth bound). The Lipschitz constant L being treated as a tuned hyperparameter further weakens the interpretation of the derived scalings as truly 'optimal'.

The column-wise scheme is only conditionally optimal: Theorem 3.7 requires a non-negativity condition on a 2r×2r linear system solution, which holds empirically for only ~80% of layers. The resulting mixture heuristic (column scaling when possible, scalar otherwise) has no theoretical support, so the end-to-end method is essentially a well-engineered hybrid rather than a provably optimal procedure.

Empirical gains are modest and sometimes within reported standard deviations. For example, on LLaMA3-8B several per-task differences vs. MoRA/HiRA (e.g., BoolQ, PIQA, WG) are small relative to ±0.5-0.9 spreads, and no significance testing is reported. The clearest win is GLUE/RTE, a small dataset, raising questions about generality of the advantage.

Scalability of the flagship method is limited: full ScaLoRA incurs O(mnr) per-iteration merge cost and ~50%+ wall-clock overhead vs. LoRA (Figure 3), so the strongest claims rest on the intermittent variant ScaLoRA-I, whose behavior depends on an amortization interval I that trades off performance (accuracy drops from 65.6 at I=1 to 63.3 at I=100). The paper is somewhat candid about this, but it narrows the practical significance at large scale.

Merging into W requires materializing and modifying the full pre-trained weight matrix, conflicting with the memory-efficient premise of PEFT (mitigated only via disk/DRAM trade-offs per the authors' discussion).

Originality is moderate: the merge-and-accumulate idea follows ReLoRA, and the initialization-view of Theorem 3.2 subsumes LoRA-GA. The genuine novelty lies in the tractable scaled-transform family and the moment-equivariance argument, which is a solid but incremental advance over the high-rank LoRA line (ReLoRA, MoRA, HiRA, LoRA-GA).

No explicit code release is promised; given the several implementation-dependent heuristics (when to switch scaling schemes, choice of I, hyperparameter L), reproducibility would benefit substantially from released code.
